19	# 论文写作风格规范
20	
21	> 核心哲学：**论文是一个有说服力的故事，不是实验报告。** 审稿人在几十秒内判断论文价值——如果 Abstract 和 Introduction 读起来像实验日志，论文就已经失败了。
22	
23	---
24	
25	## 一、总体写作哲学
26	
27	### 1.1 故事驱动，不是数据堆砌
28	
29	- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证
30	- 禁止大量实验数据堆砌——每个数字出现必须服务于叙事推进
31	- 附录内容必须在正文中有明确引用且融入叙事，禁止简单堆砌
32	- 如果附录数据对核心叙事有重大影响，根据附录数据调整论文 framing
33	
34	### 1.2 主线统一性
35	
36	- 当 idea 在研究过程中发生变化后，**必须重审全文逻辑**
37	- 常见问题：Introduction 讲的故事 A，Method 做的是故事 B，Results 又在讲故事 C
38	- 修复方式：从最终实验结论反推，重写 Introduction 的问题定义和动机
39	- 每次 idea 调整后检查：Abstract → Introduction → Method → Results → Discussion → Conclusion 是否形成一条连贯主线
40	
41	### 1.3 专有名词必须有定义
42	
43	- 首次出现的专有名词/缩写必须给出完整定义和解释
44	- Abstract 中使用的缩写也必须在 Abstract 内定义（如 LLM = Large Language Model）
45	- 不能假设读者知道你自己定义的术语——论文从来没解释过的概念不能直接使用
46	- 通用规则：如果一个非标准术语第一次出现时没有括号定义，就是写作 bug
47	
48	### 1.4 写作前必读同类优秀论文
49	
50	- 每个章节动笔前，找 **2-3 篇目标会议近 1-2 年的高分论文**作为风格参考——同类问题或同类方法皆可
51	- 重点学：
52	  - Abstract 怎么用最少篇幅讲完故事
53	  - Introduction 怎么从大问题切入到具体贡献
54	  - Related Work 怎么 positioning 自己（不是 survey）
55	  - Table/Figure 怎么压缩信息密度
56	- **不是抄袭**，是学习同行的故事节奏和审美——不同子领域叙事节奏差异很大
57	- 实操：Paper Agent 可以从 `literature_map.yaml` 中挑 `role=foundation` 或 `role=direct-competitor` 的论文，把 `{title, venue, year, abstract}` 附在 Worker 的 task_prompt 中作为概念参考；如需学习写作风格本身，让 Worker 通过 WebSearch 取得论文链接并 fetch 全文
58	
59	---
60	
61	## 二、Abstract 写作规范
62	
63	### 2.1 四个必答问题（150-250 words）
64	
65	Abstract 必须在很短的篇幅内清楚回答：
66	1. **研究什么问题** — 1-2 句话交代背景和痛点
67	2. **为什么重要** — 现有方法的不足（不用写太多）
68	3. **本文提出什么** — 核心贡献的关键机制（简要，不堆砌细节）
69	4. **结果说明什么** — 用具体实验结论支撑贡献
70	
71	### 2.2 禁忌
72	
73	- **禁止堆砌数据**：Abstract 不是 Results 的缩写。最多引用 2-3 个关键数字，要服务于 claim
74	- **

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with selection or aggregation---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where standard aggregation mechanisms break down.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks across fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B and zero-shot 72B models.
4	All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL-2003, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
5	For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
6	We identify a diagnostic cascade---instance degeneracy sets the ceiling on improvement, oracle headroom determines the opportunity, and LP compression limits exploitation---that persists under our 72B zero-shot configuration, providing, to our knowledge, the first systematic characterization of when test-time scaling succeeds or fails for NER and similar set-valued extraction tasks.
7	The diagnostic motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.006$, construction family $k{=}10$) and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$, $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.20$) under fine-tuning. Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a degeneracy decomposition confirms that SC gain vanishes when degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
8	\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with selection or aggregation---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where standard aggregation mechanisms break down.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks across fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B and zero-shot 72B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL-2003, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We identify a diagnostic cascade---instance degeneracy sets the ceiling on improvement, oracle headroom determines the opportunity, and LP compression limits exploitation---that persists under our 72B zero-shot configuration, providing, to our knowledge, the first systematic characterization of when test-time scaling succeeds or fails for NER and similar set-valued extraction tasks.
The diagnostic motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.006$, construction family $k{=}10$) and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$, $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.20$) under fine-tuning. Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a degeneracy decomposition confirms that SC gain vanishes when degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
\end{abstract}
tool_args.new_string:
\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, yet for structured information extraction (IE), where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, a persistent gap separates quality estimation from sample selection.
We ask whether entity-level agreement signals can bridge this gap.
Across seven methods spanning self-judgment, self-refinement, latent consistency, heterogeneous verification, adaptive budgeting, distillation, and supervised classification, we find that no entity-level agreement signal reliably improves selection for named entity recognition (NER), relation extraction (RE), or Text-to-SQL.
The failure is systematic: all signals yield null or negative selection gains on four RE benchmarks and SQL parsing (87.2\% output degeneracy).
A temperature ablation reveals agreement becomes actively misleading under elevated sampling (conditional $\rho{=}{-}0.048$ on Few-NERD), and a mechanistic probe identifies a gap between hidden-state frequency agreement (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] 0.87) and prompt-based self-evaluation (AUROC 0.51), an introspection boundary that surface agreement cannot cross.
These negative results delineate where self-consistency (SC) does succeed for IE: through paths that bypass entity-level agreement.
Log-probability selection improves F1 by $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.019$), entity-level construction via weighted voting gains $+1.02$\textendash$1.40$\,pp, and cross-model ensembles add $+0.42$\,pp.
Each exploits sequence-level or cross-model signals rather than entity-level self-verification.
A degeneracy decomposition confirms SC gain vanishes once output degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
\end{abstract}
